## PR and verification

I opened [PR #134](https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack/pull/134) from an isolated worktree; your existing checkout and its modified lockfile were left untouched.

The full suite passed: **61 files, 739 tests**. Typecheck and build passed, and the PR’s cold-cache Git install smoke check is green. Its release-branch update was skipped because this is a PR, so **nothing was published or released**.

## User flow after the changes

| Scenario | What Tally does |
|---|---|
| Entire’s base-checkout test command exits nonzero, but the candidate passes | Tally passes the candidate and records the baseline exit code in the attempt reason. This makes a one-off failure during baseline recording visible without mistaking it for a candidate regression. |
| Entire finds newly failing candidate tests | Tally records the failing tests and follows its existing one-time escalation flow. Entire Graph’s `verify` command runs the supplied test command and returns an adjudicated verdict. [Entire Graph command reference](https://github.com/entireio/entire-graph/blob/main/docs/commands.md) |
| Neatlogs delivery and readback succeed | Tally saves the correlated worker trace ID, as before. |
| Neatlogs is delayed or fails | Tally waits up to 20 seconds for the shared spool lock. If delivery or readback still fails, the attempt ledger and run status explain the cause—such as pending batches, HTTP auth/project errors, or traces still indexing. The task run can finish; you can retry trace delivery with `tally traces drain --run RUN_ID`. |
| The account rejects the selected model; fallback is off | Tally reports the rejected tier and stops without substituting a model. |
| The account rejects the selected model; fallback is enabled | Init lets the user choose a configured fallback tier, or scripted init can use `--model-access-fallback-tier <name>`. Tally checks that tier’s spend ceiling against the remaining budget and retries once. If the fallback is also rejected or the budget is insufficient, the task ends with a reason. Auth, network, quota, and rate-limit failures do not trigger fallback. |
| An optional integration is off | The existing opt-in behavior remains: Tally uses its local ledger and normal verifier without requiring that integration. |

Neatlogs trace listing still uses a page size of **50** with cursors; that’s the documented maximum, so raising it to 100 would not be valid. [Neatlogs pagination docs](https://docs.neatlogs.com/api-reference/pagination)

**Entire Trails are still not integrated by Tally in this PR.** Entire’s current CLI docs say project Trails mode requires `ENTIRE_PROJECT_TRAILS=1`; Tally does not set that or call the Trails commands. [Entire Project Trails CLI docs](https://github.com/entireio/cli/blob/main/docs/architecture/project-trails-cli.md)

These are code and package-install checks; I did not run a paid worker task against your live Neatlogs, Entire, or cfo.ai accounts. The published package also remains unchanged until a later release.

## Problem

PR #134 makes Neatlogs worker-drain failures visible and adds `tally traces drain`, but a live run showed that the normal completion path can still leave traces pending and require a separate manual command.

In the 2026-10-12 live test of PR #134, run `run-20261012-034213Z` processed issue [#13](https://github.com/adot-7/tally-sponsor-e2e-20261011/issues/13). The worker passed and Tally opened [test PR #14](https://github.com/adot-7/tally-sponsor-e2e-20261011/pull/14). At run completion, Neatlogs was `missing`: 26 batches were retained because another drain held the shared lock until the 20-second wait expired. Running `tally traces drain --run run-20261012-034213Z` after the worker exited delivered the batches and verified two correlated traces. No data was lost, but the run required an extra operator action to reach a verified state.

## Expected

- After worker processes and their hooks exit, Tally should retry a transiently held drain lock with a bounded post-worker recovery attempt, then perform trace read-back before reporting the final integration status.
- Never remove a live lock or acknowledge/drop a batch before Neatlogs confirms delivery. Retain pending data and show the manual recovery command if the bounded retry still cannot finish.
- When a manual recovery succeeds, keep the run summary, ledger, and dashboard consistent about current delivery status while retaining useful history of the earlier failure.

## Acceptance criteria

- Add coverage for a drain lock that remains active through the initial wait and is released after worker shutdown; retained batches are subsequently delivered and read-back verified.
- A successful retry records verified trace IDs and reports Neatlogs as `ok` without requiring the user to discover and run a second command.
- A persistent lock or export/read-back failure remains actionable, preserves the batches, and gives the user the exact recovery command.
- Document the resulting completion and recovery behavior.
EOF

Tally currently uses cfo.ai as a budget control and aggregate spend ledger. It reads the monthly budget/spend and writes tier totals plus current and cumulative run spend to the configured tables. Tally's local ledger contains richer per-task routing and attempt data, but that context is not currently published to the scenario for Ari.

As a result, Ari can report aggregate spend but has too little structured context to reliably answer organization-CFO questions such as:

- Why was a task assigned to this tier/model, and what evidence drove that decision?
- What did a particular run or issue cost, including retries and model-access fallback?
- If we priced the observed token usage at another configured model's rates, how would the estimate and budget headroom change?
- Which assumptions are list-price estimates, and which values are the actual cfo.ai budget/spend cells?

This is distinct from the cfo.ai onboarding/schema fix in #123: the tables can be created and updated, but Ari still needs a usable decision-level data contract and clear interpretation of its fields.

## Goal

Make Tally's run history and cost assumptions queryable by Ari in the selected cfo.ai scenario, so finance questions can be answered from traceable Tally data with explicit assumptions and caveats.

## Proposed scope

- Publish append-only, idempotent records keyed by `runId` and task/attempt. Include task identifier and concise title, status, size and confidence, routing tier/model/provider, configured ceiling, attempt/escalation/fallback outcome, token usage when available, estimated cost and its source, verification result, and commit/PR references.
- Publish the budget and pricing assumptions used for each run: monthly budget/spend snapshot, run cap, tier/model rates, rate source and `asOf` time, and whether a cost is measured usage or a list-price estimate.
- Give Ari scenario-level context for finding and interpreting these records. Use cfo.ai's supported scenario/table context mechanisms; do not assume that naming a table makes its meaning or caveats clear to Ari.
- Keep historical run records stable rather than overwriting them with the latest run. Do not publish secrets, raw agent transcripts, or source contents as CFO context.

## Acceptance criteria

- A dedicated Tally E2E scenario contains the documented tables/context and can be updated safely on repeated runs without duplicate task-attempt records.
- Validate Ari against representative questions about run/task spend, routing rationale, remaining budget, and a what-if that reprices observed token usage using another configured model's rates.
- Ari's answers identify the run/data and assumptions used, distinguish list-price estimates from provider invoices, and say when token/rate data is missing instead of inventing a precise result.
- Tests cover the data mapping, repeat-run/idempotency behavior, and arithmetic for at least one candidate-model comparison.

Fair point. I focused the last issue and PR on Codex because the live Neatlogs failure involved the Codex hook spool. That is a narrow recovery path; Tally’s runner choice is separate from its agent choice: it supports AO or direct runners, with Claude Code or Codex as the harness. One run proves the path you selected; it won’t necessarily exercise both harnesses. [The current setup guide](https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack/blob/main/docs/GETTING_STARTED.md) describes the supported choices.

I fetched `main` and inspected its setup flow; I did **not** create a repo or run a Tally check. Current `main` is `7509d37`, and the prebuilt GitHub `release` branch identifies that same source commit. npm’s latest is still `0.1.0`, published before that main commit, so installing from npm tests the currently published user experience, while `#release` tests the newer main build. [npm package](https://www.npmjs.com/package/tally-agents) · [release source record](https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack/blob/release/release-source.json)

PR #137 is still open and is not in that main/release build. If Neatlogs reports a pending drain during your run, the current recovery command is `tally traces drain --run <run-id>`.

## 1. Install and check the prerequisites

For the actual npm user journey:

```sh
npm install -g tally-agents@latest
tally --version
tally --help
```

To try the current main build instead, use this **instead of** the npm install above:

```sh
npm install -g 'github:Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack#release'
tally --version
```

Both may report version `0.1.0`; the release branch is built from the newer main source. The main branch itself is source-only. [The setup guide](https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack/blob/main/docs/GETTING_STARTED.md) documents both installation paths.

Check GitHub and whichever coding agent you want to use:

```sh
gh auth status

# Choose one or both:
claude auth status
codex login status

# Only needed if you plan to use AO:
ao status --json
```

If you choose `runner: direct`, AO is not required. For a real run, you need one installed, signed-in agent and GitHub access to the private test repo.

## 2. Create a private, testable repository

Run this in a terminal where you want the test checkout:

```sh
OWNER="$(gh api user --jq .login)"
REPO_NAME="tally-e2e-$(date +%Y%m%d)"

gh repo create "$OWNER/$REPO_NAME" --private --clone --add-readme
cd "$REPO_NAME"

mkdir -p src test
```

Seed a tiny project with a working test command:

```sh
cat > package.json <<'EOF'
{
  "name": "tally-e2e",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "private": true,
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": {
    "test": "node --test"
  }
}
EOF

cat > src/math.js <<'EOF'
export function add(a, b) {
  if (!Number.isFinite(a) || !Number.isFinite(b)) {
    throw new TypeError('a and b must be finite numbers');
  }
  return a + b;
}
EOF

cat > test/math.test.js <<'EOF'
import test from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { add } from '../src/math.js';

test('add returns the sum', () => {
  assert.equal(add(2, 3), 5);
});

test('add rejects non-finite inputs', () => {
  assert.throws(() => add(Infinity, 1), TypeError);
});
EOF

npm test
git status --short
git add package.json src test
git commit -m "Add minimal Tally test project"
git push
```

Stay on the repository’s default branch; `tally init` uses the current branch as its base proposal.

## 3. Add the Tally backlog

Create the label and six independent issues:

```sh
gh label create tally --description "Tally end-to-end tasks"

gh issue create --title "[Menial] Add subtraction" --label tally --body 'Implement and export subtract(a, b) in src/math.js. Match add: accept finite numbers and throw TypeError for non-finite inputs. Add tests for positive, negative, zero, and invalid values. Do not change add.'

gh issue create --title "[Menial] Format integer cents" --label tally --body 'Add formatCents(cents) in src/money.js. Return a signed decimal string with exactly two fractional digits: 1234 becomes 12.34 and -5 becomes -0.05. Reject non-safe-integer input with TypeError. Add tests; do not use locale-dependent formatting.'

gh issue create --title "[Medium] Add multiplication" --label tally --body 'Implement multiply(a, b) in src/multiply.js. Accept finite numbers, throw TypeError for non-finite inputs, and preserve normal JavaScript decimal arithmetic. Add tests in test/multiply.test.js.'

gh issue create --title "[Medium] Add division with zero handling" --label tally --body 'Implement divide(a, b) in src/divide.js. Accept finite numbers, throw TypeError for non-finite inputs, and throw RangeError when b is zero. Add tests in test/divide.test.js.'

gh issue create --title "[Complex] Summarize transactions" --label tally --body 'Implement summarizeTransactions(entries) in src/ledger-summary.js. Each entry has a non-empty category and safe-integer cents. Return { count, totalCents, byCategory }; include negative amounts, return zero totals for an empty array, and do not mutate input. Reject invalid entries with TypeError. Add tests.'

gh issue create --title "[Complex] Filter transactions" --label tally --body 'Implement filterTransactions(entries, options) in src/ledger-filter.js. Entries have category and ISO date fields. Support exact category filtering and inclusive from/to date bounds, preserve input order, return a new array, and do not mutate input. Reject invalid dates or a from date after to with a clear error. Add tests.'

gh issue list --label tally --state open
```

The `[Menial]`, `[Medium]`, and `[Complex]` prefixes are for your review. Tally sizes issues from their content and repository evidence; the `tally` label is what selects issues for the backlog.

## 4. Initialize Tally and choose integrations

From the test repo:

```sh
tally doctor
tally init --dry-run --verbose
tally init
```

Use the interactive `tally init` for this first run. Review the final summary before accepting it. The current guide covers the prompts and their defaults. [Neatlogs, Entire, and cfo.ai are optional](https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack/blob/main/docs/GETTING_STARTED.md); declining them still leaves the core issue-to-PR flow available.

Choose:

- **Runner:** `ao` if you want AO-managed sessions and AO is running; `direct` if you want Tally to start the installed agent itself without AO. Keep parallelism off for this first check.
- **Harness:** whichever agent you want to test: `claude-code`, `codex`, or `mixed`. “Mixed” does not guarantee a single run will use both.
- **Test command:** `npm test`; setup command can be blank.
- **Issue label:** `tally`.
- **Monthly/run budget:** use your chosen local fallback. The actual first-run cap is supplied below with `--budget 5`.
- **Model-access fallback:** choose a configured tier such as `middle` only if you intend to test fallback after an explicit model-access denial.

For the sponsor integrations, answer **Yes** only to the ones you want this run to prove:

- **Neatlogs:** connect the project key. Optional read access and project selection support history/read-back; worker traces also need hooks. The global hook option changes machine-wide Claude/Codex settings and traces sessions outside Tally, so review that prompt carefully.
- **Entire:** connects Graph sizing and checkpoint capture. Its repository settings need to be available on the default branch before workers inherit them; Codex also asks you to trust hooks through `/hooks`. Hosted checkpoint recall is separate and can be broken when the repository is not mirrored; that does not by itself disable Graph sizing.
- **cfo.ai:** connect, select the workspace and scenario, and separately approve any missing tables. Tally reads the monthly budget and writes run/tier spend. The richer task-level what-if context for Ari remains tracked separately in [issue #135](https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack/issues/135); this test can prove budget/spend writes, not that Ari already has a complete organizational CFO view.

Credentials belong outside the repository, under `~/.tally/.env`, not in `tally.yaml`. The config records which integrations are enabled; it should not contain tokens.

A representative config section looks like this:

```yaml
budget:
  source: cfoai # use "config" for local-only budgeting
  usd: 5         # local fallback; --budget below sets this run's cap

integrations:
  neatlogs: true
  entire: true
  cfoai: true
  slack: false
```

To change an integration later, preview and re-run init:

```sh
tally init --dry-run --verbose --entire yes
tally init --entire yes

# Or:
tally init --entire no
tally init --neatlogs no
tally init --cfoai no
```

Those flags select config options; interactive onboarding still handles logins, hook setup, and table creation. Avoid `--yes` while you expect to approve those separate steps: it uses defaults and does not perform optional browser or remote-write approvals. Turning an integration off stops Tally from using it; it does not necessarily uninstall the vendor CLI or remove repository capture settings.

Run doctor again after init:

```sh
tally doctor
```

Check that the runner and selected harness are available, and that each integration you enabled reports its status and any fix.

## 5. Plan first, then run once

Confirm the backlog and routes without starting workers:

```sh
gh issue list --label tally --state open
tally run --plan --budget 5
```

Check that the plan lists the six issues, their estimated sizes, selected tiers, ceilings, and sizing/history sources. If you want the $5 cap to cover all six, run them in **one** Tally invocation; `--budget 5` on separate invocations resets the run cap each time.

Then run the real tasks:

```sh
tally run --budget 5 --dashboard --open --port 0
```

This uses real agent accounts and may create branches and PRs; it does not merge PRs. The cap is a model-spend estimate/safety threshold, not a provider billing guarantee; in-flight usage can overshoot it. If the plan says tasks may not fit, inspect the ceilings before raising the cap.

## 6. Check what happened

After the run, inspect:

```sh
cat .tally/runs/latest/run.json
cat .tally/runs/latest/ledger.json
gh pr list --state open
```

Look for:

- One ledger row per attempt, with tier/model, result, cost estimate, ceiling, and PR URL.
- **Neatlogs:** decision trace IDs and worker trace IDs on ledger rows; the run’s integration status should explain missing/unverified traces. If a finished run has pending traces, copy its `runId` from `run.json` and use `tally traces drain --run <run-id>`.
- **Entire:** checkpoint IDs/session IDs in the run evidence and checkpoint trailers on commits. A local checkpoint alone does not prove hosted recall works.
- **cfo.ai:** updated budget/spend and tier rows in the chosen scenario. Ari’s richer what-if answers are a separate outstanding product gap, not something this run can certify.

For a first-user experience check, repeat the run with a fresh set of issues if you change integrations after creating PRs. Issues already referenced as closing issues by open PRs are excluded from later intake.

## The first-attempt failure case

A complex issue may fail verification on its first attempt and escalate, but filing a complex issue does not guarantee that outcome. To test the distinct **model-access fallback** path, set `modelAccessFallbackTier` in `tally.yaml` to an available configured tier (for example, `middle`) and use a primary model that the selected harness account is known to reject. Run only one small issue with a cap that can cover the fallback:

```sh
tally run --only '#ISSUE_NUMBER' --budget 5
```

That tests a rejected model starting at zero usage and Tally trying the configured fallback once, if the error is an explicit model-access denial. It does not simulate a worker running and then failing tests; that separate escalation depends on the first attempt’s actual result and available budget.

One last correction on scope: current main’s Neatlogs lock-recovery PR is Codex-spool-specific; the rest of the runbook is harness-neutral. The local checkout’s pre-existing `package-lock.json` change remains untouched.

content.text:
## What’s hanging

I reproduced the pause. With Neatlogs enabled, `tally run --plan --budget 5` printed the budget line and produced no plan output for 45 seconds. The live Tally process had moved past GitHub and was waiting on a connection to `app.neatlogs.com`.

With Neatlogs disabled in a temporary config outside your repo, the same plan finished in about four seconds and listed all six issues. I removed that temporary config afterward; I made no changes to Tally or the test repo.

The cause is the Neatlogs history read: its trace and span requests have no timeout, and Tally only falls back to local history if a request fails. A request that stays open can therefore leave the plan waiting indefinitely. Tally also waits for the whole plan before printing any issue decisions, so the terminal looks frozen. The relevant code is in the [Neatlogs history adapter](/home/adot/.nvm/versions/node/v20.20.2/lib/node_modules/tally-agents/dist/adapters/neatlogs-history.js:221) and the [plan output path](/home/adot/.nvm/versions/node/v20.20.2/lib/node_modules/tally-agents/dist/cli/main.js:255).

The Neatlogs onboarding did complete its checks: the SDK probe passed, read access was verified and saved, and global hooks were installed. The history read is a separate runtime step, and it’s the step that stalled. The transcript also doesn’t show you trusting the Neatlogs hooks in Codex, so future Codex-session capture may still be inactive. Trusting those hooks won’t fix the history-read hang.

The onboarding layout feedback is fair: this is a line-by-line CLI flow, not a two-column screen. `tally doctor` also reports that the Neatlogs API key is set; it doesn’t show whether history reads work or hooks are trusted.

## Entire hooks

Tally did set up Entire hooks. You approved generating the settings and committing/pushing them; the test repo’s `origin/main` has the Entire settings and Codex hook files. Then init asked whether you had trusted the hooks in Codex, and you answered `n`, so it left `integrations.entire: false`.

That trust step belongs to Codex: its current documentation says non-managed hooks must be reviewed and trusted by the user, and `/hooks` is the CLI screen for doing that. Tally can write and publish the hook configuration, but it can’t silently approve it for you. [Codex hook documentation](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/hooks) and Tally’s [Entire onboarding flow](/home/adot/.nvm/versions/node/v20.20.2/lib/node_modules/tally-agents/dist/onboarding/entire.js:143) describe that boundary.

+Tally keeps account access, data capture, repository changes, and paid work behind separate choices. A successful `tally doctor` check proves a connection is reachable; it does not approve hooks, capture, table creation, or a worker run.

content.text: I’ve completed the fix and the live, read-only integration checks. The regression suite and build passed; I’m checking the final worktree/package contents now. The test repository and your main checkout have stayed untouched.

## What I changed

I fixed the two problems behind the confusing run:

- **Neatlogs history reads could hang or time out.** The adapter requested spans for unrelated traces and could make many sequential requests. It now reads spans only for the exact legacy Tally history trace, reuses one history snapshot, and applies a 15-second deadline to the whole read. If history is unavailable, Tally falls back locally and explains that in the plan.
- **The CFO monthly balance could be misread as the available run budget.** Plans and runs now cap work at the lower of the requested/configured cap and the CFO’s remaining monthly budget. The plan spells out both numbers.

I also changed the onboarding product summary to a two-column table and added a human approval guide: [HUMAN_APPROVALS.md](/tmp/tally-fix-onboarding-20261012/docs/HUMAN_APPROVALS.md). The getting-started guide and README now explain the relevant limits and approval points.

## Checks and live evidence

The full suite passed: **61 test files, 745 tests**. Typecheck and build passed, and the package dry run includes the new docs.

In a read-only plan against your test repo, the fixed build completed, found remote Neatlogs history, read GitHub issues, and read the CFO budget. The account showed **$1.00 monthly budget, $0.3437 spent, and $0.6563 remaining**. With `--budget 5`, Tally planned two $0.30 tasks and skipped the rest because the remaining balance would not cover them. The Neatlogs history had only one small/cheap attempt, which was too little evidence to change routing; I’m not claiming it improved the model choice from that sample.

Other integration findings:

- GitHub CLI authentication worked, and Tally could read the six issues.
- CFO authentication and budget reads worked. I did not write to a scenario or run workers.
- Neatlogs’ configured key is present, and the plan confirmed remote history access. I did not send a new probe trace.
- Entire is installed and authenticated, but **Tally currently has Entire disabled**. Its status says Codex hook approval still needs review.
- The configured Codex models remain **unverified**: doctor does not send a model request, and I did not spend provider credits.
- Your Tally config selects the direct runner, so AO is not required for these runs.

The Neatlogs API documents a maximum trace page size of 50 and cursor pagination; the fixed adapter uses that limit and avoids the unnecessary span reads ([pagination](https://docs.neatlogs.com/api-reference/pagination), [authentication and scopes](https://docs.neatlogs.com/api-reference/authentication)).

## What the published npm package does

I tested the registry release, **`tally-agents@0.1.0`** ([npm release](https://www.npmjs.com/package/tally-agents/v/0.1.0)), separately from current main:

- Your current `tally.yaml` fails validation in that release because it contains newer config fields the release does not recognize.
- With those fields removed in a temporary copy, its plan showed all six tasks at $0.30 each—**$1.80 total**, despite only $0.6563 remaining in CFO.
- That release’s planner uses local price history, so its plan does not use Neatlogs history. Its Neatlogs adapter requests 100 traces, has no request deadline, and can fetch spans for unrelated traces. Neatlogs limits trace pages to 50, so a live read can fail and fall back without the newer plan’s clear history behavior.
- Its onboarding still displays integrations in the older one-line format.

So the package currently on npm does **not** include these fixes. They will require a new package release.

## Human actions still needed

Some steps must remain explicit because Tally cannot approve account access or trust hooks on your behalf:

1. **Review and trust hooks in Codex.** Open `/hooks` in the relevant repo, inspect the Neatlogs and Entire hooks, and trust only the ones you want. Codex requires that human review step ([Codex hooks documentation](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/hooks)). Entire’s capture hooks can record coding-session data, so review its privacy behavior before enabling it ([Entire security and privacy](https://entire.io/gh/entireio/cli/files/docs/security-and-privacy.md)).
2. **Enable Entire for Tally after hook trust.** Re-run `tally init` and choose Entire. If repository settings need publishing, review and approve that commit/push as part of setup.
3. **Before a real `tally run`, check the plan and budget.** A real run starts coding agents and can incur provider costs and write CFO usage records. Tally’s accounting cap is not a provider-side billing limit, and provider-reported usage can lag.
4. **Verify model access with your provider account.** Current doctor output confirms CLI sign-in, not access to each configured model.

No issues, PRs, commits, pushes, hook approvals, CFO writes, or worker/model runs were made during this work. I used an isolated worktree at `/tmp/tally-fix-onboarding-20261012`; your original checkout still has only its pre-existing `package-lock.json` change, and the test repo’s pre-existing untracked `tally.yaml` and `.tally/` remain untouched.

## PR #143

I rebased PR #143 onto the latest `main` and fixed the conflict in Neatlogs history. The resolution keeps both model-specific history matching and the bounded, shared remote read. I pushed commit `0c11bc3`.

The PR is **open and mergeable**. Its GitHub release check passes; locally, all **808 tests across 64 files**, typecheck, and build pass. I did not merge it.

## Entire: access is working; the test repo has no checkpoints yet

The Entire CLI is signed in as `adot-7`, and its repo list showed `tally-e2e-20261012` as private with admin access. The GitHub App permission was working; the missing step was creating a mirror. App access and mirroring are separate steps in [Entire’s mirror guide](https://docs.entire.io/guides/repositories/mirrors).

I created the mirror with the Entire CLI. It is ready, and Tally’s current-source `doctor` now reports checkpoint search as connected. However, a search returned zero results, and `entire checkpoint list --json` is empty for the test repo. **There is nothing to recall until a real agent run creates a checkpoint.** Once a Codex worker makes a change with the trusted Entire hooks, check it with:

```sh
entire checkpoint list --json
entire checkpoint search "a phrase from the task" --json --compact --limit 5
```

One unexpected detail: I asked for the India placement, but the mirror listing now shows **both India and US placements**. The repo remains private. Entire treats each region as a separate copy, so check whether the US placement is acceptable for this repo; its docs recommend choosing regions based on where agents run and your organization’s policy.

## Neatlogs: the delay is real, but today’s read completed

A read-only plan run from the PR branch took **11.2 seconds**. Measuring the Neatlogs reader separately showed it fetching 10 sequential pages—up to 500 traces total—with requests taking 5.5–7.8 seconds overall; one page took 2.8 seconds. All requests returned HTTP 200 in those checks.

The PR puts a 15-second deadline across the history read, so a slower read should time out and fall back instead of waiting indefinitely. It can still pause for several seconds without showing per-page progress. Neatlogs trace pages allow up to 50 items and use cursor pagination ([pagination docs](https://docs.neatlogs.com/api-reference/pagination)), so reducing the amount of history Tally scans remains a useful follow-up.

The plan showed `History source: none` **even though the Neatlogs read succeeded**. I found 11 Tally history records in the pages checked, but they all lacked a model identifier. Current `main` isolates history by model, so it correctly excludes those older records from estimates for the configured Codex models. A real run on the current code records the model with each outcome; a later plan can use matching observations. The service-account read path was accepted; Neatlogs documents `observability:read` for trace access ([authentication and scopes](https://docs.neatlogs.com/api-reference/authentication)).

To check the bounded behavior yourself using the PR code:

```sh
cd /tmp/tally-fix-onboarding-20261012
npm run tally -- run --plan --budget 5 --config /home/adot/tally-e2e-20261012/tally.yaml
```

This starts no workers. If you repeat this with the published `tally` command, note that npm’s latest is still **0.1.0**; it won’t have PR #143’s changes until a new version is released.

## What remains for a demo

**Merging PR #143 alone won’t complete the demo setup.** Your hooks are trusted, the repo is mirrored, and the integrations respond. You still need:

- A new npm release after merge for users installing `tally-agents`.
- One real Codex task to create a checkpoint and model-tagged Neatlogs outcome. I did not start one; that would incur model spend and write CFO usage.
- Model access confirmation. Doctor sees Codex signed in, but does not probe the configured models.
- Enough CFO budget for the intended demo. The read-only plan showed **$0.6563 remaining of $1.00**. With a `$5` CLI cap, it planned two `$0.30` tasks and skipped the rest; `--budget` cannot raise the live CFO limit.

For new users, hook trust and the choice to mirror a private repo into selected regions still require explicit human decisions. Tally’s current onboarding does not create the Entire mirror itself; I created this one through the CLI. The human approval points are documented in [HUMAN_APPROVALS.md](/tmp/tally-fix-onboarding-20261012/docs/HUMAN_APPROVALS.md).

content.text:
## Result

**Latest `origin/main` passed the checks and two real runs.** I tested commit `aae43fe`—including PR #143—in an isolated worktree. Typecheck and build passed; Vitest passed **815 tests across 65 files**.

Both runs completed on the direct runner and opened PRs in your private E2E repo:

- [PR #7 — Filter transactions](https://github.com/adot-7/tally-e2e-20261012/pull/7): spent **$0.0179**
- [PR #8 — Summarize transactions](https://github.com/adot-7/tally-e2e-20261012/pull/8): spent **$0.0095**

They’re open and unmerged. Total Tally-recorded spend was **$0.0274**. The live CFO scenario showed **$0.6563** available before the runs and **$0.6288** afterward; each run had a $0.30 cap.

## Sponsor integration evidence

- **Neatlogs:** Both worker traces passed remote read-back verification. After the first run, a plan for the next issue found one matching remote observation. After the second, it found two: 100% pass rate, $0.0137 average cost. Tally still chose the cheap tier because two samples are below its five-sample threshold. [Run 1 record](/home/adot/tally-e2e-20261012/.tally/runs/run-20261012-104924Z/run.json) · [Run 2 record](/home/adot/tally-e2e-20261012/.tally/runs/run-20261012-105238Z/run.json)
- **Entire:** Both mirror placements report ready: India (`aws-ap-south-1`) and US East (`aws-us-east-2`). Remote search found both sessions, and `entire checkpoint explain` retrieved their transcripts. The current-branch checkpoint list is empty because these checkpoints are on the still-open PR branches. You can demonstrate recall with:
  ```sh
  entire checkpoint search 'Filter transactions' --json --compact --limit 5
  entire checkpoint explain 01M4QVRXS5WCTP6KJN57MDZK88
  ```
- **CFO.ai:** Tally read the live monthly budget, applied the per-run caps, and recorded the run links. [Tally E2E scenario](https://app.cfo.ai/s/REDACTED) · [Budget table](https://app.cfo.ai/s/REDACTED). This verifies the budget integration; it doesn’t test Ari’s conversational what-if answers.
- **GitHub:** Authentication and PR creation worked for both tasks.

Both runs encountered Neatlogs spool lock contention on the initial drain. Tally retried after the workers exited, then verified delivery remotely; neither run failed or needed you to intervene. The end-of-run Neatlogs message can still mention missing history for the middle tier even when the plan used cheap-tier history. The plan’s `History source: remote Neatlogs` and sample counts are the clearer evidence.

## What remains

**No additional integration-code PR is indicated by these main-branch tests.** The actual npm registry release is a separate blocker for fresh users: npm’s `latest` is still `tally-agents@0.1.0` from Oct 11. I installed that registry tarball separately; it rejects the current init config because its schema doesn’t recognize `modelAccessFallbackTier` and `parallelWorkers`. Your global `tally` also reports 0.1.0, but its schema accepts those fields, so it is not the same build as the registry tarball. A versioned package release is needed before fresh npm installs get this flow.

Only the cheap model was exercised by the real runs; medium and top remain unverified. AO was off, so this tests the direct runner. Vitest passed on Node 20.20.2, though it warned that Vitest 5 declares a Node 22.12+ requirement.

## Workspace notes

The original checkout remains on `ee513f5`, while `origin/main` is `aae43fe`; I left it there because it had a pre-existing modified `package-lock.json`. Its tracked status still shows only that existing change. I did accidentally run one `npm ci` in that checkout before switching to the isolated worktree, which refreshed its ignored `node_modules`.

The published-package inspection remains under `/tmp/tally-published-e2e-20261012`. The environment’s automatic review rejected my cleanup command because `rm -f` style commands are disallowed; the directory contains only the public npm package and its dependencies.

## What’s next

Current `main` passed the real runs; I don’t see a further integration-code PR to raise from those results. The useful next check is a **fresh onboarding run** in a disposable private repo. It will show whether a new user can get from `tally init` to an issue plan, a PR, remote Neatlogs history, and an Entire checkpoint.

The existing E2E repo has two open proof PRs: [#7](https://github.com/adot-7/tally-e2e-20261012/pull/7) and [#8](https://github.com/adot-7/tally-e2e-20261012/pull/8). Keep or close them after you’ve captured what you need.

One onboarding step to pay attention to: Tally enables Entire capture, but **hosted mirror setup is separate**. Codex hook trust also requires you to approve the hooks in Codex.

## 1. Get the current `main` CLI

These commands use GitHub CLI over HTTPS, so they avoid an SSH username/password prompt.

```sh
gh auth status
# If you need to sign in:
# gh auth login --hostname github.com --web --git-protocol https

export TALLY_SRC=/tmp/tally-onboarding-main-20261012
gh repo clone Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack "$TALLY_SRC"
cd "$TALLY_SRC"
git switch main
git pull --ff-only origin main
npm ci --include=dev
```

## 2. Create a small private test repo

Run this in the same shell:

```sh
export REPO="tally-onboarding-check-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)"

cd "$HOME"
gh repo create "adot-7/$REPO" --private --clone
cd "$REPO"

npm init -y
npm pkg set scripts.test="node --test"
mkdir -p src test

cat > src/math.js <<'EOF'
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}

module.exports = { add };
EOF

cat > test/math.test.js <<'EOF'
const test = require("node:test");
const assert = require("node:assert/strict");
const { add } = require("../src/math");

test("add returns the sum", () => {
  assert.equal(add(2, 3), 5);
});
EOF

npm test
git add package.json src test
git commit -m "Add small test fixture"
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main

gh label create tally --color "7057ff" --description "Tasks for Tally"
gh issue create --title "Add subtract helper" \
  --body "Implement subtract(a, b) in src/math.js. Add a test in test/math.test.js and run npm test." \
  --label tally
gh issue create --title "Add multiply helper" \
  --body "Implement multiply(a, b) in src/math.js. Add a test in test/math.test.js and run npm test." \
  --label tally
```

## 3. Preview and run onboarding

Still from the new repo directory, preview the prompts without applying changes:

```sh
"$TALLY_SRC/node_modules/.bin/tsx" "$TALLY_SRC/cli/main.ts" init --dry-run --verbose
```

Then do the actual setup:

```sh
"$TALLY_SRC/node_modules/.bin/tsx" "$TALLY_SRC/cli/main.ts" init
```

For this test, choose `npm test`, leave setup blank, use the `tally` label, select the **direct** runner and Codex, and enable Neatlogs, Entire, and cfo.ai. Choose the dedicated **Tally E2E** CFO scenario. Keep the run cap at **$0.30**; the last check showed $0.6288 remaining in that scenario.

If init asks to commit and push the Entire settings on this disposable repo, review the listed files and approve. When it asks whether the hooks are trusted, leave that terminal waiting. In a second terminal:

```sh
cd "$HOME/$REPO"
codex
```

In Codex, enter `/hooks` and trust the Neatlogs and Entire hooks for this repo. Return to the init terminal and confirm. That trust step is a deliberate user approval.

If the Entire app doesn’t already have access to the new private repo, grant it access in GitHub’s app installation settings. Then create the hosted mirror:

```sh
entire auth status
# If needed: entire login

entire repo mirror add "/gh/adot-7/$REPO" \
  --cluster aws-ap-south-1.entire.io --timeout 5m
entire repo mirror list --name "$REPO" --json
```

## 4. Plan, run one issue, and check the evidence

Back in the repo terminal:

```sh
"$TALLY_SRC/node_modules/.bin/tsx" "$TALLY_SRC/cli/main.ts" doctor
gh issue list --state open --label tally
```

Copy the issue number for **Add subtract helper**, then use it in place of `ISSUE1`:

```sh
ISSUE1=ISSUE_NUMBER_HERE

"$TALLY_SRC/node_modules/.bin/tsx" "$TALLY_SRC/cli/main.ts" run \
  --plan --only "$ISSUE1" --budget 0.30

"$TALLY_SRC/node_modules/.bin/tsx" "$TALLY_SRC/cli/main.ts" run \
  --only "$ISSUE1" --budget 0.30 --yes
```

Save the run ID printed at the end. Then check the trace and PR:

```sh
RUN_ID=RUN_ID_FROM_OUTPUT

"$TALLY_SRC/node_modules/.bin/tsx" "$TALLY_SRC/cli/main.ts" traces drain --run "$RUN_ID"
gh pr list --state open
```

Finally, plan the second issue without starting another paid run. This checks whether Neatlogs history from the first run is available remotely:

```sh
ISSUE2=SECOND_ISSUE_NUMBER_HERE

"$TALLY_SRC/node_modules/.bin/tsx" "$TALLY_SRC/cli/main.ts" run \
  --plan --only "$ISSUE2" --budget 0.30
```

Look for `History source: remote Neatlogs` and the matching observation count. For Entire, search for the checkpoint and open it using its ID or the task commit SHA:

```sh
entire checkpoint search "Add subtract helper" --json --compact --limit 5
entire checkpoint explain CHECKPOINT_ID_OR_COMMIT_SHA
```

If this fresh run feels confusing, the likely follow-up is improving the mirror handoff and the Neatlogs status wording. The two real runs already showed the trace-delivery retry recovering automatically; no manual retry was needed.

const patch = "*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: /tmp/tally-pr-demo-evidence/README.md
@@
-Entire documents commit links as
-`https://entire.io/gh/<org>/<repo>/commit/<commit-sha>`. Tally keeps
-`checkpointUrl` null unless the CLI returns a URL; a local checkpoint does not
-by itself establish that a hosted link works.
+Entire checkpoint records live in separate Git refs, not on the task branch.
+Tally keeps the checkpoint ID and native session ID, and attaches a clickable
+Entire session link only when the Entire CLI confirms that the GitHub repo has
+a ready mirror. The link opens the session that contains the checkpoint; a
+reviewer still needs access to that repo in Entire. Without a ready mirror,
+Tally keeps the checkpoint ID available in the local ledger rather than adding
+a link that may not open.
+
+After each run has completed its Neatlogs read-back, Tally adds an evidence
+section to the generated PR body when links are available: Entire session and
+checkpoint, Neatlogs routing and worker traces, and the configured cfo.ai
+budget and spend tables. Worker trace links are added only after Tally verifies
+their read-back. These dashboard links use the viewer's existing account
+access; Tally does not publish public trace shares.
*** End Patch";
text(await tools.apply_patch(patch));

It lists generated files before asking to enable capture, then separately asks before committing those settings and pushing them to the repository's default branch. Capture settings must reach the base branch for future workers; uncommitted settings are not enough. Codex hook trust is a separate `/hooks` confirmation.
@@

Being on adds Graph and local checkpoints. **Hosted past-failure checkpoint recall needs an accessible repository mirrored to Entire.** If hosted recall is unavailable, normal planning and local capture remain available. If you skip it, local capture and normal runs remain available, but the PR shows a checkpoint ID instead of a hosted session link. Brain is a separate memory extension; Tally does not install or use it. Generated summaries are off by default and require separate approval.
@@
-| Entire | `checkpointId`, `entireSessionId`, any returned checkpoint URL, and handoff metadata. Off integrations or attempts without a captured checkpoint can legitimately have null IDs. A local checkpoint does not prove that a hosted link works. |
+| Entire | `checkpointId`, `entireSessionId`, a session URL when the repo has a ready Entire mirror, and handoff metadata. Off integrations or attempts without a captured checkpoint can legitimately have null IDs. The PR body and dashboard link to Entire only when the mirror is ready. |
*** End Patch";

content.text:
## PR and live output

I opened [Tally PR #149](https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack/pull/149), linked to issue #124. It’s based on the latest `main`, remains open, and its GitHub check passed. I haven’t merged it or published an npm tag.

The fresh live run passed issue #2 for **$0.0089** under a **$0.35** cap. Tally generated [demo PR #9](https://github.com/adot-7/tally-e2e-20261012/pull/9) and automatically added this evidence section:

> **Tally run evidence**
>
> - [Entire session and checkpoint](https://entire.io/gh/adot-7/tally-e2e-20261012/session/01a12fee-7d40-7622-9470-64acc6ae531f) — checkpoint `01M4QYY3Z9PCF513E42PB3HMJ0`
> - [Neatlogs routing trace](https://app.neatlogs.com/traces/1499055c28e408801c5876408617b965)
> - [Neatlogs worker trace](https://app.neatlogs.com/traces/951c214a1ac6475e6fc5d786beec3410)
> - [cfo.ai budget table](https://app.cfo.ai/s/REDACTED)
> - [cfo.ai spend table](https://app.cfo.ai/s/REDACTED)

` t ally doctor` reported the Entire CLI, graph, checkpoint recall, and Web mirror connected; Neatlogs and cfo.ai were connected too. The configured cheap tier succeeded in the live run, though `doctor` itself doesn’t preflight model access. CFO showed about **$0.6146** remaining afterward.

## Why checkpoints weren’t clickable

Tally already recorded checkpoint IDs and pushed checkpoint refs, but its PR publisher only put the issue description and `Closes` line in the PR body. It didn’t turn the session/checkpoint data into a hosted link, and it didn’t establish that the repository had an Entire Web mirror.

The new flow checks that the mirror is ready, then links to the **Entire session page** and shows the checkpoint ID alongside it. That’s the useful clickable view; the old checkpoint ID by itself was just text.

On onboarding, if no mirror is ready, Tally now offers an explicit mirror opt-in. Mirroring copies the repository to Entire and may ask you to choose regions. Skipping it keeps local Entire capture and checkpoint recall enabled, without claiming the checkpoint is available on the web.

## One unresolved run

A separate run on issue #1 had the agent make the change, and its six tests passed, but Tally classified the attempt as `tool-failure needs intervention` and opened no PR. Manual Entire graph verification passed; Neatlogs couldn’t provide readable failure spans, so the underlying cause remains unresolved. I’ve recorded that caveat in the source PR rather than counting it as a successful run.

The demo repository is private. Entire’s session view requires authorized repository access; Neatlogs and cfo.ai links follow their own access settings. No public Neatlogs shares are created.

## Onboarding preview

I ran the current source CLI’s `init --dry-run` in a scratch clone with Neatlogs, Entire, and cfo.ai enabled. This is the **no-write preview**; it doesn’t run the real integration setup prompts or check the live CFO budget.

```text
Optional integrations
  Integration  What it adds
  Neatlogs     Tally traces and optional history from past tasks
  Entire       Code graph sizing and local session checkpoints
  cfo.ai       Live monthly budget and spend records
Each integration is optional. You can enable one later by rerunning tally init.

Tally init proposed changes:
Runner: direct (one task at a time)
Repository: adot-7/tally-e2e-20261012 (base: main)
Test: npm test
Setup: npm ci
Issue label: tally
Budget: cfo.ai live account budget (local fallback: $40)
Integrations:
  Integration  Status
  Neatlogs     on
  Entire       on
  cfo.ai       on

Integration connection changes require separate approval.
Dry run: no changes made.
```

The live `tally doctor` run against your E2E repo reported **Entire CLI, graph plugin, checkpoint recall, Web mirror, Neatlogs key, and cfo.ai connected**. It also reported Codex connected; model access remains unverified because doctor doesn’t send a model request.

## Evidence from a real run

[PR #9](https://github.com/adot-7/tally-e2e-20261012/pull/9) has clickable links to the Entire session/checkpoint, Neatlogs routing and worker traces, and cfo.ai budget and spend tables. That demonstrates the evidence-linking work from [merged PR #149](https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack/pull/149). The test repo and its PR are private, so viewers need the appropriate GitHub and sponsor-account access.

Your Ari screenshot’s arithmetic reconciles: the latest increment is `$0.05974`, cumulative spend is `$1.07277` against a `$5` budget, and the two largest increments account for about `90.6%` of total spend. Ari can explain aggregate spend; the missing task, retry, and token details are the gap described in [open issue #135](https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack/issues/135).

There is still a run reliability gap: the earlier issue #1 attempt ended with `tool-failure: needs intervention` and produced no PR, despite the worker tests passing. So the integrations and evidence flow have working proof; the full task flow has one known failure to investigate.

## Proposed final PR, after your approval

I’d combine the frictionless Entire setup with issue #135’s CFO context work:

- If Entire is selected but its CLI is missing, offer to install it. On **yes**, use Entire’s documented installer and verify the CLI; on **no** or installation failure, explain how to continue without it. Installing the CLI would remain separate from enabling repo capture, trusting hooks, publishing settings, or configuring a mirror. [Entire installation docs](https://docs.entire.io/installation)
- Add an idempotent task/attempt ledger and pricing assumptions for Ari, then validate representative spend and model what-if questions. The data should include its source and limitations, without publishing transcripts or secrets.
- Keep the evidence links already added by PR #149.

The source `main` package is `0.2.0`; npm’s `latest` tag still points to `0.1.0`. I have not started the PR or changed source/config files. The checkout currently shows a modified `package-lock.json`, which I left untouched.

If these outputs look good, reply **“looks good”** and I’ll start the PR work.

The formatting can be improved further. You can also make the connected green text and things like that. You can add green dots you know it make it better in that sense for tally doctor, tally in it, whatever also we can have the install help for entire B applied to the other integrations as well, right? So why not do that also the context for the CFO agents add as much as possible and package all of this into one PR and then push it by push it I mean create a PR don merge it. also show how youre gonna format it so i see. its not just format but ptrettyfying it ig. see the tally theme it is orange like if i am not wrong, the logo so we can follow something like that. basically make the experience good.

I’ll build this as one reviewable PR on a fresh worktree from current `main`, leaving the existing checkout and its `package-lock.json` edit alone. I’ll first inspect how each integration is detected and connected, then implement the colored Tally styling, opt-in install/setup help for each integration, and richer CFO context. I’ll show you the proposed output style before I create the PR, then test and push the branch without merging it.

[PR #150](https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack/pull/150) · [npm package](https://www.npmjs.com/package/tally-agents) · [release source manifest](https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack/blob/release/release-source.json)

### Demo repo

I created the public [Penny Ledger repo](https://github.com/adot-7/penny-ledger), a small personal-finance toolkit with a working transaction ledger. Its baseline `npm test` passes four tests. The five open issues all have the `tally` label and specific acceptance criteria:

1. [Format integer cents as USD](https://github.com/adot-7/penny-ledger/issues/1) — small
2. [Filter by category and date](https://github.com/adot-7/penny-ledger/issues/2) — medium
3. [Export escaped CSV](https://github.com/adot-7/penny-ledger/issues/3) — medium
4. [Build a monthly income and expense summary](https://github.com/adot-7/penny-ledger/issues/4) — complex
5. [Validate and deduplicate imported transactions](https://github.com/adot-7/penny-ledger/issues/5) — complex

I left difficulty out of the issue labels so Tally can size them itself. The main Tally checkout was not changed.

### Install the current onboarding

Your current global CLI showed `0.1.0`. To install the prebuilt release branch that includes PR #150:

```sh
npm uninstall -g tally-agents
npm install -g 'github:Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack#release'
rehash
tally --version
```

The quotes matter in zsh. Once a new npm version is published from the current main commit, use this instead:

```sh
npm uninstall -g tally-agents
npm install -g tally-agents@latest
rehash
tally --version
```

You can check the registry with `npm view tally-agents@latest version`. The project’s [getting-started guide](https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack/blob/main/docs/GETTING_STARTED.md) documents both the npm and prebuilt `#release` install paths.

### Set up Penny Ledger

```sh
gh auth status
gh repo clone adot-7/penny-ledger
cd penny-ledger
npm test
codex login status
tally doctor
tally init
```

During `tally init`:

- `npm test` should be detected; leave setup blank.
- Keep the issue label as `tally`.
- Enable Neatlogs, Entire, and cfo.ai.
- Use **direct** mode for a simple, sequential run; AO is not required.
- Keep Codex selected (it is the default).
- Choose the CFO workspace and scenario you intend to show. Your previous choice was **Included Whippet → Tally E2E**.
